title: India-EU Free Trade Agreement: From Negotiation to Signature and Ratification

CURRENT AFFAIRS 202
India-EU Free Trade Agreement: From Negotiation to Signature and
Ratification
Category
GS
Date
Quick rule
International Relations / Economy
GS II / GS III
12 Sep 2026
Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• The European Commission placed the India-EU FTA before the Council on 11 September 2026 for authorisation to
sign and conclude the agreement.
• Negotiations had concluded on 27 January 2026; Council approval and European Parliament consent are key EU-side
steps before conclusion.
• The agreement is economically important because it combines tariff liberalisation with rules on standards, services,
procurement, sustainability and market access.
WHY IN NEWS
• The move from negotiated text to the EU's formal approval process makes the FTA an immediate trade-policy issue
rather than a continuing negotiation story.
• For India, implementation capacity on rules of origin, standards and non-tariff barriers will determine how much
exporters actually use the preferences.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• India and the EU relaunched FTA negotiations in June 2022.
• Negotiations for the FTA concluded on 27 January 2026.
• The European Commission submitted proposals to the Council for signature and conclusion on 11 September 2026.
• The Council must authorise signature on the EU side.
• The European Parliament must give consent before conclusion of the agreement.
• The text becomes binding only after each side completes its internal legal procedures for entry into force.
• The EU says tariffs would be eliminated or reduced on more than 96% of EU goods exports to India.
• EU-India goods trade was about EUR118 billion in 2025.
• EU-India services trade was about EUR67 billion in 2024.
• EU FDI stock in India was about EUR132.8 billion in 2024.
• India's major interests include textiles, leather, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and services.
• Rules of origin determine whether a product qualifies for preferential tariff treatment.
• Non-tariff measures such as standards, testing and certification can limit preference utilisation.
• The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is relevant to carbon-intensive Indian exports.
• The India-EU Trade and Technology Council complements trade ties in digital and green technologies.

PRELIMS
• FTA is distinct from the separately negotiated Investment Protection Agreement and GI agreement.
• European Commission negotiates; Council authorises signature; European Parliament gives consent.
• Rules of origin prevent simple trans-shipment from obtaining preferences.
• CBAM is an EU carbon-border instrument, not a customs union.
• Mode 4 under GATS concerns movement of natural persons supplying services.
• Trade agreements can reduce tariffs but do not automatically remove all regulatory barriers.
QUICK REVISION
Recall the sequence: negotiations concluded -> Commission proposal -> Council authorisation -> European Parliament
consent -> internal procedures -> entry into force. Link the FTA with rules of origin, CBAM, standards, services and the
India-EU Trade and Technology Council.
PROBABLE OBJECTIVE QUESTION
With reference to the above topic, consider the following statements:
1. The European Parliament must consent before the EU concludes the agreement.
2. Rules of origin help determine eligibility for preferential tariffs.
3. The India-EU FTA automatically brings the Investment Protection Agreement into force.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 2 and 3 only
(b) 1 and 2 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Answer: (b) 1 and 2 only
Explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The investment-protection track is separate and does not automatically enter
into force with the FTA.

PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
Discuss the opportunities and implementation challenges arising from the India-EU Free Trade Agreement. How can
India improve utilisation of negotiated trade preferences?
MODEL ANSWER - ~300 WORDS
INTRODUCTION
The move from negotiated text to the EU's formal approval process makes the FTA an immediate trade-policy issue
rather than a continuing negotiation story. The agreement is economically important because it combines tariff
liberalisation with rules on standards, services, procurement, sustainability and market access.
SIGNIFICANCE
• The FTA can diversify markets at a time of global protectionism and supply-chain fragmentation.
• Lower tariffs can improve competitiveness of labour-intensive and manufacturing exports.
• Services and professional mobility can deepen India's role in high-value trade.
CHALLENGES
• EU sustainability, product-safety and carbon requirements may operate as costly non-tariff barriers.
• Sensitive Indian sectors need calibrated adjustment and safeguards.
• Low awareness of rules of origin and certification can produce low preference utilisation.
WAY FORWARD
• Build exporter support for origin documentation, testing and certification.
• Use the Trade and Technology Council to address digital, clean-tech and standards issues.
• Track preference utilisation sector by sector and create rapid grievance channels.
CONCLUSION
The FTA's success will be measured not by the size of the tariff schedule alone, but by whether Indian firms can convert
legal market access into durable exports and investment.
India should therefore prepare before formal entry into force rather than wait for tariff cuts to begin. Export promotion
councils can map product-level opportunities, while laboratories and certification bodies need capacity to meet
European technical requirements. Customs authorities and firms must understand origin documentation so preferences
are not lost through procedural errors. A monitoring dashboard can compare eligible trade with actual preference claims
and identify sectors where standards, logistics or information gaps suppress utilisation. This turns the agreement from a
diplomatic achievement into an instrument of export competitiveness.
